analysis.one_liner: Creates government-managed personal investment accounts for new Social Security participants, seeded with $1,000 at birth.
analysis.headline: The bill drew zero cosponsors and never received a hearing or vote; it died in a House Ways and Means subcommittee when the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a personal investment account for every person issued a Social Security number starting in 2006, seeded by a one-time $1,000 payment from the Treasury. It would let anyone add tax-deductible contributions of up to $5,000 a year, invest the money in a small menu of government-run index and bond funds similar to federal employees' Thrift Savings Plan, and eventually buy a retirement annuity from a private insurer. It also specifies an unusual funding source: Social Security tax money paid on wages of workers whose earnings cannot count toward benefits, topped up by revenue from taxing Social Security benefits.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone born from 2006 onward would get a $1,000 starter account at birth that compounds over decades. Savers would gain a new deduction worth up to $5,000 a year, which is worth the most to higher-income households. Private insurers would gain a new market, because the bill requires the government to purchase annuity contracts from insurance companies when account holders retire. The fund structure is managed by the federal board that runs the Thrift Savings Plan, keeping management costs low.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Future retirees, savers, and annuity insurers

how_it_helps.text: Every new Social Security number holder would receive a $1,000 initial contribution from the Treasury general fund into a personal account [S3].
Account holders could deduct up to $5,000 a year of contributions to their account, allowed whether or not they itemize deductions [S3].

Accounts would be invested by the Federal Retirement Thrift Investment Board, which manages the low-cost Thrift Savings Plan for federal employees, with a choice of government securities, fixed income, and stock index funds [S3].
Retirees could choose an annuity, staggered withdrawals, or a rollover to another retirement plan, with joint-and-survivor protections for spouses by default [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The Treasury general fund would pay $1,000 for every child born each year, several billion dollars annually. The bill's primary financing redirects Social Security tax revenue collected on wages of workers whose earnings cannot qualify them for benefits, and secondary financing takes revenue from the taxation of Social Security benefits, meaning the existing system's income would be reduced. When an account holder dies, the portion of the balance traceable to the government's $1,000 is returned to the Treasury.
analysis.who_pays_short: Treasury and Social Security's funding base

drawbacks.text: The primary financing source is Social Security tax money paid on wages of individuals who do not satisfy the legal-residence criterion, reducing trust fund income, with any shortfall made up from revenue generated by taxing Social Security benefits [S3].
Account holders choosing the bond or stock funds must sign an acknowledgment that the investment is at their own risk and is not protected or guaranteed by the government against loss [S3].
The $5,000-a-year deduction is worth the most to taxpayers in higher brackets, so the largest tax benefits flow to higher-income households [S3].

Regular Social Security benefit payments would be drawn first from the retiree's individual account balance, with the traditional system covering only any excess, restructuring how the guaranteed benefit is funded [S3].
Annuities must be purchased from private insurance companies, creating a mandated market for the insurance industry paid for out of the public trust fund [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The $1,000-at-birth seed account is a genuine, universal benefit, and the Thrift Savings Plan-style fund structure keeps fees low. But the financing is the weak point: the bill pays for those accounts partly out of Social Security's own tax receipts, weakening the existing system's income while shifting investment risk onto individuals for the stock funds. The tax deduction, the bill's biggest fiscal cost after the seed money, skews toward higher earners. An honest supporter would have to acknowledge that the bill makes the system's finances harder, not easier, even before accounting for administrative costs paid from fund earnings.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and then to its Social Security subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or vote until the 109th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Thomas Petri, a Republican from Wisconsin, introduced the bill on April 21, 2005 [S1].
The House referred it to the Committee on Ways and Means the day it was introduced [S5].
On May 4, 2005 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Social Security, and no further action was ever taken [S5].
The bill attracted zero cosponsors in the House [S4].
The 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, with the bill still pending in committee, so it died without a vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained materially. The existing Social Security structure was left untouched, and the industries that would have gained a new annuity and account-contribution market received nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; Social Security went unchanged

for.name: Rep. Thomas E. Petri
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it, but attracted no cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 21, 2005 and never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill.

against.name: Subcommittee on Social Security
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on May 4, 2005 and took no further action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No votes occurred and the bill drew no cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split is on the record.

industries.note: The bill would require the government to purchase an annuity contract from a private insurance company for every retiring account holder, creating a guaranteed stream of customers funded from the public trust fund. The bill does impose bonding and contract-term requirements on the insurers [S3].

Fixed income investments would be selected by qualified professional asset managers, and a new flow of contributions up to $10,000 a year per person would enter the investment industry. However, the account structure mimics the Thrift Savings Plan's low-cost index approach, limiting fee capture [S3].
The up-to-$5,000 annual deduction for contributions is worth the most to taxpayers in the top brackets, and contributions could total $10,000 a year per account [S3].
